title: Rambour: original righteousness natural as native, not as flowing from nature's powers, like natural knowledge of God
source_text: XXXII. Denique Ramburtius in Sedanensium Thesium Syntagmate Disputatione de imagine Dei in homine, & justitia Originali. Thesi vigesima septima sic de hac quaestione sententiam suam pronunciat, Nos statuimus justitiam Originalem complecti totam hominis integritatem & sanctitatem, eamque homini fuisse naturalem: ita ut in Adae natura, simul atque extitit, insitum fuerit diligere Deum, eique obtemperare, hocque dono excelluisse hominem statim atque conditus est. Quod ita non volumus accipi ac si ex naturae viribus profluxerit haec sanctitas; sed quod nativa fuerit homini haec integritas: ita ut in eo per naturam, ut a Deo conditus est, & in hoc statu substitit, nulli fuerint motus inordinati: quemadmodum naturalem dicimus esse aliquam cognitionem Dei, quatenus nihil est tam naturale, quam quod ita naturae insidet, ut sine ejus, ut sic dicam, ejuratione non possit amoveri. Haec igitur justitia fulsit in Adamo simul ac exortus est, nihilque huic justitiae tepugnans expertus est.
pass_a_gloss: Finally Rambour in the Syntagma of the Sedan Theses, Disputation on the image of God in man, and Original justice. In Thesis twenty-seven pronounces his opinion on this question thus, We hold that Original justice comprises the whole integrity and sanctity of man, and that it was natural to man: so that in Adam's nature, as soon as it came into being, it was implanted to love God, and obey him, and that man excelled in this gift as soon as he was founded. Which we do not want to be taken thus as if this sanctity flowed from the powers of nature; but that this integrity was native to man: so that in him by nature, as he was founded by God, and stood in this state, there were no inordinate motions: just as we say that some knowledge of God is natural, insofar as nothing is so natural, as what so sits in nature, that without its, so to speak, abjuration it cannot be removed. This justice therefore shone in Adam as soon as he arose, and he experienced nothing tepugnans [so the print; read repugnans, repugnant] to this justice.
pass_b_english: Finally Abraham Rambour, in the Syntagma of Sedan Theses, disputation on the image of God in man and original righteousness, thesis 27, gives his view on the question in these words: "We hold that original righteousness includes the whole integrity and holiness of man, and that it was natural to him. Loving God and obeying him were planted in Adam's nature from the moment it existed, and man excelled in this gift from the moment he was made.

"We do not want this to be taken as though this holiness flowed from the powers of nature, but in the sense that this integrity was native to man, so that in him, by nature as God made him and while he stood in that state, there were no disordered movements. In the same way we call some knowledge of God natural, since nothing is so natural as what is so lodged in nature that it cannot be removed without, so to speak, nature's renouncing it on oath. This righteousness, then, shone in Adam as soon as he came into being, and he felt nothing in himself that resisted it."

choices.why: The print reads 'tepugnans', a misprint for 'repugnans'; Pass B follows 'repugnans'.
